We (in my lab) have tried to be measured in our approach to talking about aperiodic analyses - including adopting measuring ECG when possible now - because there are so many sources of aperiodic activity: neural, ECG, respiration, skin conductance, muscle activity, electrode impedances, room noise, electronics noise, etc. The authors discuss this all very clearly, and I commend them on that. We, as a field, should move more toward a model where we can account for all of those sources of noise together. DOI: [10.7554/eLife.100605.3.sa3](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.100605.3.sa3)

Summary:

Schmidt et al., aimed to provide an extremely comprehensive demonstration of the influence cardiac electromagnetic fields have on the relationship between age and the aperiodic slope measured from electroencephalographic (EEG) and magnetoencephalographic (MEG) data.

Strengths:

Schmidt et al., used a multiverse approach to show that the cardiac influence on this relationship is considerable, by testing a wide range of different analysis parameters (including extensive testing of different frequency ranges assessed to determine the aperiodic fit), algorithms (including different artifact reduction approaches and different aperiodic fitting algorithms), and multiple large datasets to provide conclusions that are robust to the vast majority of potential experimental variations.

The study showed that across these different analytical variations, the cardiac contribution to aperiodic activity measured using EEG and MEG is considerable, and likely influences the relationship between aperiodic activity and age to a greater extent than the influence of neural activity.

Their findings have significant implications for all future research that aims to assess aperiodic neural activity, suggesting control for the influence of cardiac fields is essential.

Weaknesses:

The authors have addressed the weaknesses of their study in their manuscript. Most alternative explanations for their results have been explored to ensure their conclusions are robust and are not explained by unexplored confounds. Minor potential weaknesses are:

(1) The number of electrodes used in the EEG analyses was on the lower side, and as such, the results do not confirm that the influence of ECG on the 1/f activity in the EEG is high even for higher density EEG montages where ICA may provide better performance at removing cardiac components (as noted by the authors). Having noted this potential weakness, I doubt the effects of cardiac activity can be completely mitigated with current methods, even in higher-density EEG montages.

(2) Head movements were used as a proxy for muscle activity. However, this may imperfectly address the potential influence of muscle activity on the slope in the EEG activity. As such, remaining muscle artifacts may have affected some of the results, particularly those that included high frequency ranges in the aperiodic estimate. Perhaps if muscle activity were left in the EEG data, it could have disrupted the ability to detect a relationship between age and 1/f slope in a way that didn't disrupt the same relationship in the cardiac data. However, I doubt this would reverse the overall conclusions given the number of converging results, including in lower frequency bands. The authors also note this potential weakness and suggest how future research might address it.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ghinda et al., 2020 and Mostile et al., 2019 demonstrating disorder-related modulation.

claims.claim: Aperiodic activity is present in recordings of cardiac activity measured using ECG.
claims.source: However, aperiodic activity is not only present in recordings of neural activity, but also part of other physiological signals such as cardiac and muscle activity, commonly measured using electrocardiography (ECG Saul et al., 1988) and electromyography (Kozhemiako et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Saul et al., 1988 demonstrating aperiodic activity in ECG recordings.

claims.claim: Aperiodic activity is present in recordings of muscle activity measured using electromyography.
claims.source: However, aperiodic activity is not only present in recordings of neural activity, but also part of other physiological signals such as cardiac and muscle activity, commonly measured using electrocardiography (ECG Saul et al., 1988) and electromyography (Kozhemiako et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 demonstrating aperiodic activity in EMG recordings.

claims.claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by aging.
claims.source: Interestingly, and mostly overlooked by the neuroscience community (see Figure 1C), aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006), different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003) and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001; see also Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Beckers et al., 2006 and demonstrated in the manuscript's own analyses shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep).
claims.source: Interestingly, and mostly overlooked by the neuroscience community (see Figure 1C), aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006), different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003) and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001; see also Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Kozhemiako et al., 2022 and Penzel et al., 2003 demonstrating cognitive state modulation in ECG.

claims.claim: Aperiodic activity measured using ECG is modulated by disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy.
claims.source: Interestingly, and mostly overlooked by the neuroscience community (see Figure 1C), aperiodic activity measured using ECG (often referred to as power law or 1/f activity) is modulated by similar factors as neural aperiodic activity, including aging (Beckers et al., 2006), different cognitive states (e.g. awake vs. sleep Kozhemiako et al., 2022; Penzel et al., 2003) and disorders such as Parkinson's disease and epilepsy (Ansakorpi et al., 2002; Haapaniemi et al., 2001; see also Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Ansakorpi et al., 2002 and Haapaniemi et al., 2001 demonstrating disorder-related modulation in ECG.

claims.claim: Via volume conduction, cardiac activity can be captured in both invasive and non-invasive recordings of neural activity.
claims.source: Furthermore, it is well-known that, via volume conduction, cardiac activity can also be captured in both invasive and non-invasive recordings of neural activity (Dirlich et al., 1997; Jousmäki and Hari, 1996; Kern et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Dirlich et al., 1997; Jousmäki and Hari, 1996; Kern et al., 2013 and represents established knowledge.

claims.claim: It is considered best practice to measure and remove cardiac activity from M/EEG recordings.
claims.source: Hence, it is also considered best practice to measure and remove cardiac activity from M/EEG recordings (Gross et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Gross et al., 2013 and represents a methodological standard in the field.

claims.claim: Only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed.
claims.source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: Only 16.5% of EEG studies measure ECG.
claims.source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: 45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity.
claims.source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured.
claims.source: However, an analysis of openly accessible M/EEG articles that investigate aperiodic activity (NArticles = 279; see Methods - Literature Analysis for further details) revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention that cardiac activity was removed and only 16.5% measure ECG (45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% of MEG studies mention that ECG was measured; see Figure 1E,F).
claims.evidence: This is based on the literature analysis conducted by the authors, with results shown in Figure 1E,F.

claims.claim: Investigations of aperiodic activity vary strongly by both the upper and lower bounds and the general width of the analyzed frequency ranges.
claims.source: Additionally, investigations of aperiodic activity vary strongly by both the upper and lower bounds and the general width of the analyzed frequency ranges (Figure 1G-I).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the literature analysis shown in Figure 1G-I.

claims.claim: Physiological signals (e.g. cardiac activity) may have varying impacts across frequency ranges—for instance, exerting a stronger influence on lower frequencies than on higher ones.
claims.source: This further complicates the comparison of results across studies as physiological signals (e.g. cardiac activity) may have varying impacts across frequency ranges—for instance, exerting a stronger influence on lower frequencies than on higher ones.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the frequency-dependent effects observed in the study's analyses.

claims.claim: The spectral slope flattened with age over a vast amount of different frequency ranges in ECG recordings.
claims.source: Our results show that the spectral slope flattened with age over a vast amount of different frequency ranges (see Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis of ECG data from four age-diverse populations, with results shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: An age-related steepening of the spectral slope was observed in one dataset (ECG Dataset 3 - CamCAN) in the low-frequency range (0.25–12 Hz).
claims.source: However, we also noted an age-related steepening of the spectral slope in one dataset (ECG Dataset 3 - CamCAN) in the low-frequency range (0.25–12 Hz, see Discussion).
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis of ECG Dataset 3, representing an exception to the general flattening trend.

claims.claim: Spectral slopes in lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz) were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4–74.6% of all investigated indices) than spectral slopes in higher frequency ranges (16–30.01% of all investigated indices).
claims.source: Overall, spectral slopes in lower frequency ranges were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4–74.6% percent of all investigated indices) than spectral slopes in higher frequency ranges (16–30.01% percent of all investigated indices; see Figure 2D).
claims.evidence: This is based on the exploratory analysis relating spectral slopes to 90 different indices of heart rate variability, with results shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In the lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz), spectral slopes were consistently related to most measures of heart rate variability including fractal, multifractal, time and frequency domain analyses as well as indices extracted from the Poincaré plot.
claims.source: In the lower frequency ranges (0.25–20 Hz), spectral slopes were consistently related to most measures of heart rate variability; that is significant effects were detected in all four datasets (see Figure 2D). This includes fractal, multifractal, time and frequency domain analyses as well as indices extracted from the Poincaré plot.
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis relating spectral slopes to heart rate variability measures, with results shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: In the higher frequency ranges (10–145 Hz), spectral slopes were most consistently related to fractal and time domain indices of heart rate variability, but not so much to frequency-domain indices assessing spectral power in frequency ranges <0.4 Hz.
claims.source: In the higher frequency ranges (10–145 Hz), spectral slopes were most consistently related to fractal and time domain indices of heart rate variability, but not so much to frequency-domain indices assessing spectral power in frequency ranges <0.4 Hz.
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis relating spectral slopes to heart rate variability measures across different frequency ranges.

claims.claim: Spectral slopes >10 Hz carry meaningful information about cardiac activity that is largely distinct from the frequency-domain information that is commonly investigated using ECG.
claims.source: This suggests that spectral slopes >10 Hz carry meaningful information about cardiac activity that is largely distinct from the frequency-domain information that is commonly investigated using ECG.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the differential relationships between spectral slopes in different frequency ranges and heart rate variability measures.

claims.claim: The direction of the association between age and aperiodic ECG activity is largely identical to that reported for age and aperiodic EEG activity.
claims.source: Importantly, the direction of the association between age and aperiodic ECG activity is largely identical to that reported for age and aperiodic EEG activity (Donoghue et al., 2020; Voytek et al., 2015), motivating the investigation of these relationships in combined neural and cardiac measurements.
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the current ECG results with prior EEG/ECoG findings cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: If ECG components are not removed via ICA, the ECG signal is captured equally strong at zero-time lags both in EEG and MEG recordings.
claims.source: Our results show that if ECG components are not removed via ICA, the ECG signal is captured equally strong at zero-time lags both in EEG and MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,C,D).
claims.evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 3A,C,D.

claims.claim: After removing ECG-related components from the data, TRF peaks emerged (although reduced) at zero-time lags in EEG, but not in MEG recordings.
claims.source: Even after removing ECG-related components from the data, TRF peaks emerged (although reduced) at zero-time lags in EEG, but not in MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,B).
claims.evidence: This is based on the temporal response function analysis shown in Figure 3A,B.

claims.claim: Reconstruction (decoding) of the ECG signal was reduced, but remained above chance even after rejecting the ICA signal using ECG both in MEG and EEG recordings.
claims.source: Furthermore, reconstruction (decoding) of the ECG signal was reduced, but remained above chance even after rejecting the ICA signal using ECG both in MEG and EEG recordings (r>0).
claims.evidence: This is based on the decoding analysis shown in Figure 3C,D.

claims.claim: The presence of the ECG signal was more pronounced in EEG compared to MEG recordings, after removing ECG-related components.
claims.source: Interestingly, the presence of the ECG signal was more pronounced in EEG compared to MEG recordings, after removing ECG-related components (βstandardized (EEG > MEG)=0.97, HDI = [0.42, 1.52]; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of residual ECG signal in EEG vs MEG after ICA, shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: ECG-related components extracted from MEG recordings were more related to the ECG signal than the components extracted from the EEG.
claims.source: Additionally, ECG-related components extracted from MEG recordings were more related to the ECG signal than the components extracted from the EEG (βstandardized (EEG > MEG)=–0.76, HDI = [-1.35,–0.18]; Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is based on statistical comparison of ECG component correlations in MEG vs EEG, shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: Neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG as opposed to MEG recordings.
claims.source: These results show that (A) residual ECG activity remains in surface neural recordings, even after applying a very sensitive threshold to detect and remove ECG components via ICA and (B) neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG as opposed to MEG recordings (see Figure 3A,C,D), resulting in more residual (after ICA) ECG-related activity in EEG recordings.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the TRF and decoding analyses showing more residual ECG in EEG after ICA.

claims.claim: Even if the PQRST-Complex is barely visible in the combined time domain signal, the resulting power spectrum can be heavily affected by simulated changes in aperiodic cardiac activity.
claims.source: Combining both cardiac and neural time series data shows that even if the PQRST-Complex is barely visible in the combined time domain signal, the resulting power spectrum can be heavily affected by simulated changes in aperiodic cardiac activity (see Figure 3F,G).
claims.evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 3F,G demonstrating the impact of cardiac aperiodic activity on combined spectra.

claims.claim: Over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions.
claims.source: This analysis, which is depicted in Figure 4, shows that over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions (see Figure 4B) with 'steepening effects' observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis of age effects on spectral slopes across multiple conditions and frequency ranges, shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: Steepening effects were observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
claims.source: This analysis, which is depicted in Figure 4, shows that over a broad amount of individual fitting ranges and sensors, aging resulted in a steepening of spectral slopes across conditions (see Figure 4B) with 'steepening effects' observed in 25% of the slope fits in MEGECG not rejected, 0.5% in MEGECG rejected, and 60% for MEGECG components.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of effects across processing options shown in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Null effects were observed in 13% of the options for MEGECG not rejected, 30% in MEGECG rejected, and 7% for MEGECG components.
claims.source: The second largest category of effects was 'null effects' in 13% of the options for MEGECG not rejected, 30% in MEGECG rejected, and 7% for MEGECG components.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of null effects across processing options.

claims.claim: Flattening effects in the spectral slope were found for 0.16% of the processing options in MEGECG not rejected, 0.3% in MEGECG rejected, and 0.46% in MEGECG components.
claims.source: However, we also found 'flattening effects' in the spectral slope for 0.16% of the processing options in MEGECG not rejected, 0.3% in MEGECG rejected, and 0.46% in MEGECG components.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of flattening effects across processing options.

claims.claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope occurred mainly at centrally and parietally located electrodes in lower frequency ranges between 0.5 and 45 Hz.
claims.source: However, despite the large amount of age-related steepening effects, we also noted age-related flattening in spectral slopes that occurred mainly at centrally and parietally located electrodes in lower frequency ranges between 0.5 and 45 Hz (see Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: This is based on the spatial and frequency-specific analysis of flattening effects shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: The observed flattening results overlap both in frequency range and recording site with some of the results previously reported in the literature.
claims.source: Importantly, these results overlap both in frequency range and recording site with some of the results previously reported in the literature (Voytek et al., 2015; Tröndle et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This is based on comparison of the current findings with prior literature cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: A flattening of spectral slopes with age can be observed at some of the previously reported frequency ranges (~0.5–45 Hz) and spatial locations (on central, parietal, and occipital sensors).
claims.source: In sum, this analysis suggests that a flattening of spectral slopes with age can be observed at some of the previously reported frequency ranges (~0.5–45 Hz) and spatial locations (on central, parietal, and occipital sensors).
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings regarding flattening effects and their spatial/frequency characteristics.

claims.claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope represented only 0.3% of effects across all processing settings (conditions, sensors, and frequency ranges).
claims.source: However, these results represented only 0.3% of effects across all processing settings (conditions, sensors, and frequency ranges).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of flattening effects across all processing options.

claims.claim: When restrictively looking only at the investigated frequency ranges between 0.5 and 50 Hz, only 1.2% (0.4% after maxfilter) of effects across these residual settings were showing an age-related flattening of the spectral slope.
claims.source: Even when restrictively looking only at the investigated frequency ranges between 0.5 and 50 Hz, only 1.2% (0.4% after maxfilter see Figure 4—figure supplement 7) of effects across these residual settings were showing an age-related flattening of the spectral slope.
claims.evidence: This is based on quantification of flattening effects in a restricted frequency range, with maxfilter results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: Age-related flattening of the spectral slope is tied to specific recording sites and frequency ranges.
claims.source: This suggests that age-related flattening of the spectral slope is tied to specific recording sites and frequency ranges.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial and frequency-specific patterns of flattening effects observed in the data.

claims.claim: Age-related steepening/flattening of the spectral slope in the MEG is both dependent on the investigated frequency range and the sensor selection.
claims.source: So far, we have shown that age-related steepening/flattening of the spectral slope in the MEG is both dependent on the investigated frequency range and the sensor selection.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of findings from the analyses across different frequency ranges and sensor locations.

claims.claim: Aperiodic brain activity (MEGECG rejected), at some frequency ranges, changes with age independently of cardiac activity (MEGECG component) and vice versa.
claims.source: Some of the observed age-related flattening and steepening effects were solely present in one of the tested conditions (see Figure 4H). This suggests that aperiodic brain activity (MEGECG rejected), at some frequency ranges, changes with age independently of cardiac activity (MEGECG component) and vice versa.
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis of condition-specific effects shown in Figure 4H.

claims.claim: When adding both MEGECG component and MEGECG rejected as predictors, age-related flattening effects were reduced, yielding no longer significant flattening results.
claims.source: The analysis revealed that when adding both MEGECG component and MEGECG rejected as predictors, age-related flattening effects were reduced, yielding no longer significant flattening results (see Figure 4B; upper panel).
claims.evidence: This is based on the multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 4I (upper panel).

claims.claim: In the case of the observed steepening effects, significant effects for MEGECG components remained in 98.75% of the tested frequency ranges.
claims.source: However, in case of the observed steepening effects, significant effects for MEGECG components remained in 98.75% of the tested frequency ranges (see Figure 4B; lower panel).
claims.evidence: This is based on the multiple regression analysis shown in Figure 4I (lower panel).

claims.claim: Whether or not aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and the selected frequency range.
claims.source: In sum, these results suggest that whether or not aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and the selected frequency range.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the frequency- and location-dependent patterns of cardiac and neural contributions to age-related changes.

claims.claim: On the grand average across channels, the spectral slope was slightly steeper in older subjects even before spectral parametrization.
claims.source: First, we conducted a median split of age to compare the raw power spectra averaged across channels (see Figure 4—figure supplement 1). This shows that on the grand average across channels, the spectral slope was slightly steeper in older subjects even before spectral parametrization.
claims.evidence: This is based on the control analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: On the grand average across sensors, slightly stronger steepening effects were observed for the MEGECG not rejected data compared to MEGECG rejected when not cleaning the data using SSS and vice versa.
claims.source: On the grand average across sensors, slightly stronger steepening effects were observed for the MEGECG not rejected data compared to MEGECG rejected when not cleaning the data using SSS and vice versa (see Figure 4—figure supplement 5 for a comparison).
claims.evidence: This is based on the comparison of results with and without SSS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: On the level of single sensors, the application of SSS resulted in a further reduction of both flattening and steepening effects in all conditions except for MEGECG components, where we noted a 20% increase in steepening effects.
claims.source: On the level of single sensors, the application of SSS resulted in a further reduction of both flattening and steepening effects in all conditions except for MEGECG components, where we noted a 20% increase in steepening effects (see Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: This is based on the single-sensor analysis with SSS shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: The age-related steepening effects occur robustly in the MEG.
claims.source: While all these control analyses indicate that the age-related steepening effects occur robustly in the MEG, it is unclear whether they can be exclusively attributed to cardiac activity.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the multiple control analyses conducted.

claims.claim: The topography of the observed steepening effects is present across the scalp and prominent at frontal and temporal sensors around the MEG helmet.
claims.source: Crucially, the topography of the observed steepening effects is present across the scalp and prominent at frontal and temporal sensors around the MEG helmet (albeit also observable at central locations; see MEGECG Components).
claims.evidence: This is based on the spatial distribution of steepening effects observed in the analyses.

claims.claim: Head movements increased significantly with aging.
claims.source: While head movements increased significantly with aging (βstandardized=0.23, HDI = [0.18, 0.28], see Figure 4—figure supplement 8), it was not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in the spectral slope (see Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
claims.evidence: This is based on the control analysis using head movement as a covariate, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claims.claim: Head movements were not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in the spectral slope.
claims.source: While head movements increased significantly with aging (βstandardized=0.23, HDI = [0.18, 0.28], see Figure 4—figure supplement 8), it was not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in the spectral slope (see Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
claims.evidence: This is based on the control analysis using head movement as a covariate, shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claims.claim: There were no significant age-related steepening/flattening across the investigated frequency ranges in vertical and horizontal EOG channels.
claims.source: We further investigated age-related changes to the spectral slope of the vertical and horizontal EOG channels indicating no significant age-related steepening/flattening across the investigated frequency ranges (see Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
claims.evidence: This is based on the control analysis of EOG channels shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claims.claim: The discrepancy between the current findings and previous findings showing flattening can potentially be explained by multiple factors including physiologically measured 1/f noise differently affecting magnetic and electric recording devices, preprocessing choices, fitting ranges for the 1/f slope, electrode selection etc.
claims.source: This discrepancy can potentially be explained by multiple factors including physiologically measured 1 /f noise differently affecting magnetic and electric recording devices (Dehghani et al., 2010), preprocessing choices, fitting ranges for the 1 /f slope, electrode selection etc. (see discussion).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential explanations for the discrepancy, with citation to Dehghani et al., 2010.

claims.claim: A consistent flattening of the aperiodic slope for cardiac activity was observed in the delay period of a working memory task.
claims.source: Interestingly, akin to the EEG results reported by Donoghue et al., 2020, we observed a consistent flattening of the aperiodic slope for cardiac activity in the delay period (see Figure 5B,D; βstandardized=0.23, HDI = [0.16, 0.32]).
claims.evidence: This is based on the working memory analysis shown in Figure 5B,D.

claims.claim: The flattening effect of the slope was modulated by cognitive load.
claims.source: Furthermore, upon comparing the change of slope relative to the baseline period across different levels of co,gnitive load we noticed that the flattening effect of the slope was modulated by cognitive load (see Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is based on the working memory analysis comparing different load conditions shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: The slope flattened the most in the condition with the highest working memory load (13 items).
claims.source: The slope flattened the most in the condition with the highest working memory load (13 items; βstandardized=0.42, HDI = [0.33, 0.52]), followed by the high load (9 items; βstandardized=0.39, HDI = [0.29, 0.48]) and the low load condition (5 items; βstandardized=0.25, HDI = [0.15, 0.35]).
claims.evidence: This is based on the working memory analysis comparing different load conditions.

claims.claim: Previous research has shown scaling differences in the spectral slope between MEG and EEG recordings.
claims.source: Previous research has shown scaling differences in the spectral slope between MEG and EEG recordings (Dehghani et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Dehghani et al., 2010.

claims.claim: These scaling differences are partly widespread (overall flatter sloped spectra in MEG data) and partly regionally specific (steeper sloped spectra at vertex in MEG compared to EEG recordings and vice versa at frontal regions).
claims.source: These scaling differences are partly widespread (overall flatter sloped spectra in MEG data) and partly regionally specific (steeper sloped spectra at vertex in MEG compared to EEG recordings and vice versa at frontal regions).
claims.evidence: This is based on prior research cited in the manuscript.

claims.claim: These observations have been linked to non-resistive properties of tissue (i.e. the propagation of the electric field through tissue is frequency dependent).
claims.source: These observations have been linked to non-resistive properties of tissue (i.e. the propagation of the electric field through tissue is frequency dependent Dehghani et al., 2010; Bedard et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Dehghani et al., 2010 and Bedard et al., 2017.

claims.claim: Magnetic field recordings are not distorted by the tissue conductivity of the scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain.
claims.source: This differently affects the signal recorded using MEG and EEG, as magnetic field recordings are not distorted by the tissue conductivity of the scalp, skull, cerebrospinal fluid, and brain (Singh, 2014).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Singh, 2014 and represents established knowledge about MEG vs EEG.

claims.claim: Under the hypothesis that frequency scaling differences may emerge in relation to the space/frequency structure of the recorded activity, lower frequencies are suggested to involve synchronous activity in larger patches of cortex, whereas higher frequencies involve synchronous activity in smaller cortical patches.
claims.source: An alternative, but not exclusive, hypothesis suggests that even under the assumption of a purely resistive medium (which is unlikely Bedard et al., 2022; Gomes et al., 2016), frequency scaling differences between MEG and EEG may emerge in relation to the space/frequency structure of the recorded activity (Bénar et al., 2019). Under this hypothesis, lower frequencies are suggested to involve synchronous activity in larger patches of cortex, whereas higher frequencies involve synchronous activity in smaller cortical patches.
claims.evidence: This is based on the hypothesis proposed by Bénar et al., 2019.

claims.claim: EEG typically integrates activity over larger volumes than MEG, resulting in differently shaped spectra across both recording methods.
claims.source: Bénar et al., 2019 demonstrate that EEG typically integrates activity over larger volumes than MEG, resulting in differently shaped spectra across both recording methods.
claims.evidence: This is based on the findings of Bénar et al., 2019.

claims.claim: During aging, both changes in conductive tissue properties and functional connectivity occur.
claims.source: During aging, both changes in conductive tissue properties (Mohammed et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018) and functional connectivity occur (Deery et al., 2023).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to Mohammed et al., 2017; Thomas et al., 2018; and Deery et al., 2023.

claims.claim: An interaction between several factors that differently affect MEG and EEG (e.g. age-related changes in non-resistive properties of tissue and in functional connectivity) may potentially explain differently shaped spectra in MEG compared to EEG recordings.
claims.source: Hypothetically, an interaction between several factors that differently affect MEG and EEG (e.g. age-related changes in non-resistive properties of tissue and in functional connectivity) may therefore potentially explain differently shaped spectra in MEG compared to EEG recordings.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential mechanisms explaining the observed differences.

claims.claim: Aperiodic activity may not change strictly linearly as we are ageing, and studies looking at younger age groups may capture different aspects of aging (e.g. brain maturation) than those looking at older subjects.
claims.source: Differences in electric and magnetic field recordings aside, aperiodic activity may not change strictly linearly as we are ageing, and studies looking at younger age groups (e.g. <22; Tröndle et al., 2022) may capture different aspects of aging (e.g. brain maturation) than those looking at older subjects (>18 years; our sample).
claims.evidence: This is speculation about potential non-linear age effects, with citation to Tröndle et al., 2022.

claims.claim: A recent report shows some first evidence of an interesting putatively non-linear relationship with age in the sensorimotor cortex for resting recordings.
claims.source: A recent report even shows some first evidence of an interesting putatively non-linear relationship with age in the sensorimotor cortex for resting recordings (Cross et al., 2024).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citation to Cross et al., 2024.

claims.claim: An age-related steepening of the ECG was only noted at a frequency range between ~0.25 and 12 Hz making it an unlikely explanation of all the effects detected in the MEG that span frequency ranges vastly exceeding the 0.25–12 Hz range.

results.result: A literature analysis of 279 M/EEG studies investigating aperiodic activity revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies explicitly mention cardiac activity removal and only 16.5% measure ECG, while 45.9% of MEG studies removed cardiac activity and 31.1% measured ECG. Additionally, investigations vary strongly in the frequency ranges analyzed.
results.evaluation: Claims C22-C26 are based on a systematic literature analysis of 279 articles with explicit methodology described. The findings are presented with specific percentages and visualized in Figure 1E-I, providing transparent documentation of the analysis approach and results.

results.result: Analysis of ECG data from four age-diverse populations (N=2286) showed that spectral slopes flattened with age across most frequency ranges (0.25-145 Hz), with one exception showing steepening in the CamCAN dataset at 0.25-12 Hz. Lower frequency spectral slopes (0.25-20 Hz) were more consistently related to heart rate variability indices (39.4-74.6%) than higher frequency slopes (16-30.01%).
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C33 are supported by analyses across four independent ECG datasets with large sample sizes, with results visualized in Figure 2. The relationship to 90 different HRV indices provides convergent validity, though the steepening in one dataset (C29) requires further investigation.

results.result: Temporal response function analysis of concurrent MEG/EEG and ECG recordings (N=20) demonstrated that ECG signals are captured at zero-time lags in both modalities. After ICA-based ECG component removal, residual ECG activity remained in both MEG and EEG, but was significantly more pronounced in EEG (β=0.97, HDI=[0.42, 1.52]), indicating that neural and cardiac activity are more difficult to separate in EEG than MEG.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C41 are supported by TRF analysis and decoding models shown in Figure 3A-D with appropriate statistical testing. The small sample size (N=20) is a limitation, but the convergent evidence from multiple analytical approaches (TRF peaks, decoding accuracy, component correlations) strengthens the conclusions.

results.result: Analysis of MEG data (N=627) across 102 sensors and multiple frequency ranges revealed predominantly age-related steepening of spectral slopes (60% in ECG components, 25% in ECG not rejected, 0.5% in ECG rejected conditions). Age-related flattening was observed in only 0.3% of all processing settings, occurring mainly at central/parietal electrodes in 0.5-45 Hz range, overlapping with some prior literature findings but representing a minority of effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C52 are supported by comprehensive analysis across multiple processing options shown in Figure 4, with extensive control analyses (Figure 4 supplements 1-8). The unexpected predominance of steepening effects contradicts prior EEG literature, which the authors acknowledge and address through multiple control analyses and discussion of MEG vs EEG differences.

results.result: Multiple regression analysis revealed that age-related changes in aperiodic activity show both independent and shared contributions from cardiac and neural sources depending on frequency range and recording site. When both MEG ECG component and MEG ECG rejected were used as predictors, flattening effects were eliminated, but steepening effects for ECG components remained significant in 98.75% of tested frequency ranges.
results.evaluation: Claims C54-C57 are supported by multiple regression analyses shown in Figure 4H-I. The statistical approach appropriately tests for unique variance contributions, though the interpretation is complicated by the unexpected direction of effects (steepening vs. flattening) requiring careful consideration of MEG-specific factors.

results.result: Multiple control analyses confirmed the robustness of age-related steepening effects in MEG across different processing pipelines (with/without SSS), spectral parameterization methods (IRASA vs FOOOF), and in an independent dataset (N=655). The effects were not explained by head movements (β=0.23 for age-movement relationship) or EOG activity, with topography prominent at frontal/temporal sensors.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C65 are supported by extensive control analyses shown in Figure 4 supplements 1-8, including replication in an independent dataset. The convergence across multiple analytical approaches and datasets strengthens confidence in the robustness of the steepening effects, though their interpretation remains complex.

results.result: In a working memory paradigm (N=48), the aperiodic slope of ECG recordings showed consistent flattening during the delay period (β=0.23, HDI=[0.16, 0.32]), with the effect modulated by cognitive load. The slope flattened most in the highest load condition (13 items: β=0.42), followed by high load (9 items: β=0.39) and low load (5 items: β=0.25).
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 are supported by analysis of ECG data during a working memory task shown in Figure 5, with appropriate statistical testing. This demonstrates that cardiac aperiodic activity is modulated by cognitive state, extending beyond the age-related effects that are the main focus. However, this is presented as preliminary/outlook analysis.

results.result: The study demonstrates that the aperiodic signal recorded via surface electrodes/sensors originates from multiple physiological sources, with cardiac and neural contributions varying by frequency range and recording site.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C88, and C107 represent the primary conclusion of the manuscript, supported by convergent evidence from multiple analyses including ECG-MEG relationships, ICA separation limitations, frequency-dependent effects, and multiple regression models. This is the central finding integrating all other results.

results.result: Common artifact rejection approaches using ICA may not be sufficient to separate cardiac from neural activity, with ICA working worse in EEG compared to MEG recordings.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C82, and C105 are supported by the TRF analysis showing residual ECG activity after ICA (Figure 3), with convergent evidence from decoding models. The conclusion is appropriately cautious given the methodological limitations of ICA discussed in the manuscript.

results.result: Significant parts of age-related changes in aperiodic activity normally interpreted as neural can be explained by cardiac activity, with the extent depending on recording site and frequency range.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C8, and C108 are supported by the multiple regression analyses (Figure 4H-I) and the comprehensive frequency/sensor-specific analyses. This represents a major finding with important implications for interpretation of prior literature, though the unexpected steepening effects complicate interpretation.

results.result: Background claims establishing that aperiodic activity with 1/f characteristics is present across multiple recording modalities (ECoG, MEG/EEG, fMRI, ECG, EMG) and is modulated by age, cognitive states, and disorders in both neural and cardiac recordings, with cardiac activity captured in neural recordings via volume conduction.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C21 represent established knowledge from prior literature, appropriately cited throughout. These provide the scientific foundation and motivation for the current study. The literature analysis (C22-C26) provides novel quantification of how these established practices are actually implemented.

results.result: The direction of association between age and aperiodic ECG activity is largely identical to that reported for age and aperiodic EEG activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C35 is complicated by the finding that most ECG datasets showed flattening with age (consistent with prior EEG literature), but one dataset (CamCAN) showed steepening at low frequencies (C29), and the MEG analysis predominantly showed steepening. This inconsistency requires further investigation to determine whether the similarity holds across modalities and conditions.

results.result: Simulation results demonstrate that even when the PQRST-Complex is barely visible in combined time domain signals, the resulting power spectrum can be heavily affected by simulated changes in aperiodic cardiac activity.
results.evaluation: Claim C42 is supported by simulation results in Figure 3F-G. While simulations have limitations in representing real physiological complexity, they effectively illustrate the principle that cardiac aperiodic activity can influence combined spectra even when not visually apparent in time domain.

results.result: Discussion of potential explanations for discrepancies between current MEG findings (predominantly steepening) and prior EEG findings (predominantly flattening), including differences in how magnetic vs electric fields are affected by tissue properties, age-related changes in tissue conductivity and connectivity, potential non-linear age effects, and sensitivity to preprocessing decisions.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C81 represent speculative discussion of potential mechanisms, appropriately cited where relevant. While these provide plausible explanations for the unexpected findings, they remain hypotheses requiring direct testing. The authors appropriately acknowledge uncertainty and call for future research.

results.result: Discussion of factors affecting ICA effectiveness in separating cardiac from neural activity, including sensor number, non-Gaussianity assumptions, component quality, and referencing choices, with linked mastoid referencing shown to be effective but potentially problematic for temporal activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are supported by appropriate citations and represent methodological considerations relevant to the field. These provide important context for interpreting the ICA results and recommendations for future studies.

results.result: Discussion of implications for interpreting drug effects on aperiodic activity, noting that neural and vascular processes interact, that propofol/ketamine affect both neural activity and heart rate variability, and that residual cardiac activity after ICA may confound interpretation of drug-induced changes in 'neural' aperiodic activity.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C99 are appropriately cited and represent important implications of the current findings for interpreting prior pharmacological studies. The speculation about potential confounding (C99) is appropriately cautious and calls for future research rather than making definitive claims.

results.result: Discussion of additional confounding factors including muscle activity (EMG) potentially influencing spectral slopes, cardiac activity captured in ECoG recordings, and debates about whether periodic activity should be detrended using FOOOF or IRASA.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C103 are appropriately cited and acknowledge important limitations and considerations. These represent honest discussion of factors beyond the scope of the current study that may affect interpretation of aperiodic activity.

results.result: Recommendations that changes in aperiodic activity of peripheral and neural signals are co-modulated by similar factors, that ICA-based methods may not provide complete separation, and that conflating cardiac and neural contributions should be avoided.
results.evaluation: Claims C104, C106, and C109 represent appropriate conclusions and recommendations based on the study findings. These are supported by the empirical results and provide actionable guidance for future research.

results.result: Methodological details about sample characteristics (1282 MEG recordings, age 18-88 years) and ethical approvals from Cambridge and Salzburg ethics committees with informed consent obtained.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C110-C112 represent standard methodological reporting that is verifiable and appropriately documented. These provide necessary transparency about sample and ethical procedures.

results.result: A literature analysis of 279 M/EEG articles investigating aperiodic activity revealed that only 17.1% of EEG studies and 45.9% of MEG studies explicitly mention removing cardiac activity, with even fewer measuring ECG (16.5% for EEG, 31.1% for MEG).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question this literature analysis finding. One reviewer specifically noted 'The literature analysis is very clever, and expanded upon from any other prior version I've seen,' indicating acceptance of these descriptive statistics about the field's practices.

results.result: Analysis of ECG data from four age-diverse populations showed that spectral slopes generally flattened with age across multiple frequency ranges, with slopes in lower frequency ranges (0.25-20 Hz) more consistently related to heart rate variability indices than slopes in higher frequency ranges (10-145 Hz).
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted these ECG findings without critique. One reviewer noted the study 'report[s] age effects on aperiodic cardiac activity derived from ECG in low and high-frequency ranges in roughly 2300 participants from four different sites,' acknowledging the robustness of the dataset and findings.

results.result: Temporal response function (TRF) analysis demonstrated that cardiac activity is captured in both EEG and MEG recordings, and importantly, residual ECG activity remains even after ICA-based artifact rejection. The separation of cardiac from neural activity was more difficult in EEG compared to MEG recordings.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly endorsed these findings. One reviewer stated the authors 'demonstrate that cardiac activity is instantaneously reflected in neural recordings, even after applying ICA analysis to remove cardiac activity. This was more strongly the case for EEG than MEG data.' Another noted the study shows 'residual ECG activity remains in surface neural recordings, even after applying a very sensitive threshold.'

results.result: A comprehensive multiverse analysis across different frequency ranges, sensors, and processing conditions revealed that aging predominantly resulted in steepening (rather than flattening) of spectral slopes in MEG data. Age-related flattening was observed in only 0.3% of all processing settings, occurring mainly at central and parietal electrodes in lower frequency ranges (0.5-45 Hz).
results.evaluation: Reviewers strongly supported this finding. One reviewer noted the authors 'used a multiverse approach to show that the cardiac influence on this relationship is considerable, by testing a wide range of different analysis parameters.' Another stated the study 'demonstrate[s] effects of aging on the spectral slope in the currently largest MEG dataset with equal age distribution available' and commended 'their efforts of replicating observed effects in another large MEG dataset.'

results.result: Multiple regression analyses revealed that some age-related changes in aperiodic activity were uniquely linked to either cardiac or brain activity, while others were present in both signals. Whether aperiodic brain activity changes independently from cardiac activity with age depends on the recording site and selected frequency range, demonstrating that the aperiodic signal originates from multiple physiological sources.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted this core conclusion. The editor's summary stated the study provides 'compelling evidence that age-related differences in aperiodic EEG/MEG signals can be driven by cardiac rather than brain activity.' One reviewer noted the authors 'show that across these different analytical variations, the cardiac contribution to aperiodic activity measured using EEG and MEG is considerable, and likely influences the relationship between aperiodic activity and age to a greater extent than the influence of neural activity.'

results.result: Analysis of a working memory task revealed that the aperiodic slope of cardiac activity flattened during the delay period, with this flattening effect modulated by cognitive load (strongest for 13 items, followed by 9 items, then 5 items).
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically praised this analysis, stating 'Previously I recommended that the[y] push even further, and they added the current Figure 5 analysis of event-related changes in the ECG during working memory. In my opinion this result practically warrants a separate paper its own!' This enthusiastic endorsement indicates strong support for the finding.

results.result: Control analyses showed that while head movements increased significantly with aging, they were not sufficient to explain the observed steepening or flattening effects in spectral slopes. Additionally, no significant age-related changes were found in EOG channels.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged these control analyses positively. One reviewer noted the authors' 'efforts of replicating observed effects in another large MEG dataset and considering potential confounding by ocular activity, head movements, or preprocessing methods are commendable and highly valuable to the community.' However, one reviewer noted a minor weakness: 'Head movements were used as a proxy for muscle activity. However, this may imperfectly address the potential influence of muscle activity.'

results.result: Simulation results demonstrated that even when the PQRST-Complex is barely visible in the combined time domain signal, the resulting power spectrum can be heavily affected by simulated changes in aperiodic cardiac activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not critique this simulation analysis. One reviewer noted the manuscript provides 'a very compelling, convincing, thorough, and measured set of analyses,' which would encompass the simulation results shown in Figure 3F,G.

results.result: The authors discuss multiple potential explanations for the discrepancy between their findings (predominantly steepening) and previous literature (flattening), including differences between MEG and EEG in how they are affected by tissue properties, frequency scaling differences, age-related changes in tissue conductivity and functional connectivity, and potential non-linear age effects.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged this discussion positively. One reviewer stated 'The authors discuss their findings in-depth and give recommendations for the separation of physiological and neural sources of aperiodic activity.' Another noted 'While the study's aim is well-motivated and analyses rigorously conducted, it remains vague what is reflected in the ECG at higher frequency ranges that contributed to the confounding of the age effects in the neural data. However, the authors address this issue in their discussion.'

results.result: The authors discuss various factors affecting ICA effectiveness in separating cardiac from neural signals, including the number of sensors, assumptions about source non-Gaussianity, component quality, and the effects of different referencing schemes (particularly linked mastoid referencing).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this discussion. One reviewer noted the authors 'discuss this all very clearly' regarding the multiple sources of aperiodic activity and methodological considerations. The discussion of ICA limitations is part of the broader methodological commentary that reviewers found valuable.

results.result: The authors discuss how the E/I balance hypothesis for aperiodic activity (based on AMPA/GABA ratios) may be complicated by the fact that drugs like propofol and ketamine affect both neural activity and heart rate variability, and that cardiac activity may remain in EEG signals even after ICA, potentially conflating drug-induced effects.
results.evaluation: One reviewer specifically praised this discussion: 'I also very much appreciate the authors' excellent commentary regarding the physiological effects that pharmacological challenges such as propofol and ketamine also have on non-neural (autonomic) functions such as ECG.' This indicates strong reviewer support for this interpretive discussion.

results.result: Literature analysis revealed that investigations of aperiodic activity vary strongly in the frequency ranges analyzed, and physiological signals like cardiac activity may have varying impacts across frequency ranges.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question this finding from the literature analysis. One reviewer praised 'The literature analysis is very clever,' which would include these observations about methodological variability in the field.

OpenEval notes the steepening in CamCAN dataset requires investigation; peer reviewers accepted findings without critique.

Perfect agreement on cognitive modulation findings (C67-C69). Both strongly support the working memory task results. OpenEval notes this is preliminary/outlook analysis; peer reviewer enthusiastically endorsed it, suggesting it 'practically warrants a separate paper.'

Perfect agreement on simulation results (C42). Both support the simulation demonstrating cardiac influence on combined spectra. OpenEval acknowledges simulation limitations; peer reviewers found analyses 'compelling, convincing, thorough, and measured.'

Perfect agreement on methodological considerations (C83-C87). Both support the discussion of ICA limitations and recommendations. OpenEval notes appropriate citations; peer reviewers found the discussion 'very clear' regarding multiple sources of aperiodic activity.

Strong agreement on MEG findings (C43-C52). Both support the multiverse analysis showing cardiac influence. OpenEval notes unexpected steepening contradicts EEG literature; peer reviewers commended the multiverse approach and replication efforts. Peer review includes C53 not in OpenEval grouping.

OpenEval emphasizes explicit methodology; peer reviewer praised it as 'very clever, and expanded upon from any other prior version.' OpenEval includes C26 which peer review addresses separately.

Agreement on mechanistic discussion (C66, C70-C78). Both acknowledge this as appropriate speculative discussion. Agreement on TRF/decoding findings (C36-C41) but different scope. Both support evidence of residual cardiac activity after ICA. OpenEval focuses on TRF analysis claims; peer review additionally includes broader conclusions (C82, C98, C105) about ICA limitations and cardiac influence.

Agreement on regression analyses (C54-C57) but different scope. Both support unique variance contributions. OpenEval focuses on statistical approach; peer review additionally includes core conclusions (C88, C107, C108) about cardiac vs. neural contributions to age effects.
